Global strong solutions for the triangular Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto cross-diffusion system in three dimensions and parabolic regularisation for increasing functions

Hector Bouton ††thanks: Email: hector.bouton@ens.psl.eu
Université Paris Cité and Sorbonne Université, CNRS, IMJ-PRG, F-75013 Paris, France    Laurent Desvillettes ††thanks: Email: desvillettes@imj-prg.fr
Université Paris Cité and Sorbonne Université, CNRS and IUF, IMJ-PRG, F-75013 Paris, France.    Helge Dietert ††thanks: Email: helge.dietert@imj-prg.fr
Université Paris Cité and Sorbonne Université, CNRS, IMJ-PRG, F-75013 Paris, France.
Abstract

We prove the existence of global strong solutions to the triangular Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto (SKT) cross-diffusion system with Lokta-Volterra reaction terms in three dimensions. A key part is the independent careful study of the parabolic equation a​∂tw−Δ​w=fa\partial_{t}w-\Delta w=f with a rough coefficient aa, homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, and the special assumption ∂tw≥0\partial_{t}w\geq 0. By the same method, we obtain estimates for solutions to reaction-diffusion systems modelling reversible chemistry.

1 Introduction

The Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto (SKT) system [36] is a popular cross-diffusion model from Biology where it is used in population dynamics [9]. A common form is a triangular cross-diffusion system with two unknowns u:=u⁡(t,x)≥0,v:=v⁡(t,x)≥0u:=u(t,x)\geq 0,v:=v(t,x)\geq 0 modelling the concentration of two species. The evolution is prescribed by

{∂tu−Δ⁡[(d1+σ​v)​u]=fu​(u,v),∂tv−d2​Δ​v=fv​(u,v),\left\{\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}u-\Delta[(d_{1}+\sigma v)u]=f_{u}(u,v),\\ \partial_{t}v-d_{2}\,\Delta v=f_{v}(u,v),\\ \end{aligned}\right. (1)

where d1,d2>0d_{1},d_{2}>0 are constant diffusion rates, σ>0\sigma>0 is a coupling constant, and fuf_{u} and fvf_{v} are Lotka-Volterra type terms modelling competition, that is

fu​(u,v)\displaystyle f_{u}(u,v) =u⁡(ru−d11​u−d12​v),\displaystyle=u\,(r_{u}-d_{11}\,u-d_{12}\,v), (2)
fv​(u,v)\displaystyle f_{v}(u,v) =v⁡(rv−d21​u−d22​v),\displaystyle=v\,(r_{v}-d_{21}\,u-d_{22}\,v), (3)

where ru,rv≥0r_{u},r_{v}\geq 0, di​j>0d_{ij}>0, for i,j=1,2i,j=1,2. We also write μ:=d1+σ​v\mu:=d_{1}+\sigma v.

The system is defined on a smooth bounded domain Ω\Omega of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and endowed with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions

∇v⋅n→(x)=0 and ∇[(d1+σv)u]⋅n→(x)=0 for (t,x)∈ℝ+×∂Ω,\nabla v\cdot\vec{n}(x)=0\quad\text{ and }\nabla[(d_{1}+\sigma v)u]\cdot\vec{n}(x)=0\quad\quad\text{ for }(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\partial\Omega, (4)

together with initial conditions:

u⁡(0,⋅)=uin,v⁡(0,⋅)=vin.u(0,\cdot)=u_{\mathrm{in}},\qquad\qquad v(0,\cdot)=v_{\mathrm{in}}. (5)

The existence of global strong solutions in three dimensions has been a long open problem even though there is a strong interest in this cross-diffusion system. Previously, the theory of global strong solutions was only developed in one or two dimensions in [29, 9]. For higher dimensions there were only results (about global strong solutions) when the cross-diffusion is small, see [7], or when self-diffusion is added, see [6, 39, 40]. Notice that existence of weak solutions is easy to obtain in the triangular case for all dimensions (cf. for example [9, 11]). The non-triangular case is completely different and entropy functionals play there a very important role ([5, 10]). Finally, we refer to [16] for an example of use of De Giorgi type methods for cross-diffusion equations belonging to the same class as the SKT system.

This work shows the global existence of strong solutions in dimensions d≤4d\leq 4 for the triangular system (without self-diffusion and for cross-diffusion of arbitrary size):

Theorem 1.

Let d≤4d\leq 4 and Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a smooth (𝒞2\mathscr{C}^{2}) bounded domain, let d1,d2,σ>0d_{1},d_{2},\sigma>0, ru,rv≥0r_{u},r_{v}\geq 0, di​j>0d_{ij}>0 for i,j=1,2i,j=1,2. We suppose that uin,vin≥0u_{\mathrm{in}},v_{\mathrm{in}}\geq 0 are initial data which lie in 𝒞2​(Ω¯)\mathscr{C}^{2}(\overline{\Omega}) and are compatible with the Neumann boundary condition.

Then, there exists a global (defined on ℝ+×Ω\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Omega) strong (that is, all terms appearing in the equation are defined a.e.) solution to system (1)–(5).

Another consequence of our strategy is a new and very quick proof of existence of strong global solutions (for general initial data) in dimension d≤4d\leq 4, to a classical quadratic system of reaction diffusion coming out of reversible chemistry.

Namely, we consider here the unknowns ui:=ui​(t,x)≥0u_{i}:=u_{i}(t,x)\geq 0, with i=1,…,4i=1,\dots,4, and the set of equations

∂tui−di​Δ​ui=(−1)i​(u1​u3−u2​u4),\partial_{t}u_{i}-d_{i}\,\Delta u_{i}=(-1)^{i}\,(u_{1}\,u_{3}-u_{2}\,u_{4}), (6)

with di>0d_{i}>0, defined on a smooth bounded domain Ω\Omega of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, together with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions and initial conditions:

∇ui​(t,x)⋅n→​(x)=0 for ​(t,x)∈ℝ+×∂Ω,ui​(0,⋅)=uiin,\nabla u_{i}(t,x)\cdot\vec{n}(x)=0\quad\text{ for }(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\partial\Omega,\qquad u_{i}(0,\cdot)=u_{i}^{\mathrm{in}}, (7)

and we prove the following proposition:

Theorem 2.

Let d≤4d\leq 4 and Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a smooth (𝒞2\mathscr{C}^{2}) bounded domain. Let di>0d_{i}>0 be constant diffusion rates, and suppose that the initial data uiin≥0u_{i}^{\mathrm{in}}\geq 0 lie in 𝒞2​(Ω¯)\mathscr{C}^{2}(\overline{\Omega}) and are compatible with the homogeneous Neumann boundary condition of (7).

Then there exists a global (defined on ℝ+×Ω\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Omega) strong (that is, all terms appearing in the equation are defined a.e.) solution to system (6), (7).

Existence of strong solutions for this system in all dimension dd was obtained by different methods in [4, 14, 37], following the pioneering works [18, 19] in the whole space.

The specificity of our new proof is to be extremely short and self-contained. Moreover, the constants can be explicitly estimated (for example, the quadratic nonlinearity could be replaced by a nonlinearity behaving like a power 2+β2+\beta, where β>0\beta>0 can be explicitly estimated in terms of the diffusion rates did_{i}). One drawback however is that it does not cover the cases when d≥5d\geq 5. The methods that we use are much closer to those of [4, 14] than those of [37, 18, 19].

We also provide a more general result (Proposition 19) of existence of global strong solutions in dimension d≤4d\leq 4 for reaction-diffusion systems with mass dissipation, improving recent results on the same kind of systems obtained in [31, 14, 15]. More details and references are provided in Section 4.2. Among the systems which can be treated, we present a system coming from the reversible chemical reaction b1​S1+…+bm​Sm⇌Sm+1+Sm+2b_{1}S_{1}+...+b_{m}S_{m}\rightleftharpoons S_{m+1}+S_{m+2}, where m∈ℕ∖{0}m\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\} and for i∈1,…,mi\in 1,\dots,m, we have bi∈ℕ∖{0}b_{i}\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}. This system writes

{∂tum+1−dm+1​Δ​um+1=∏i=1muibi−um+1​um+2,∂tum+2−dm+2​Δ​um+2=∏i=1muibi−um+1​um+2,∂tui−di​Δ​ui=−bi​(∏i=1muibi−um+1​um+2) for i=1,…,m.\left\{\begin{lgathered}\partial_{t}u_{m+1}-d_{m+1}\Delta u_{m+1}=\prod_{i=1}^{m}u_{i}^{b_{i}}-u_{m+1}\,u_{m+2},\\ \partial_{t}u_{m+2}-d_{m+2}\Delta u_{m+2}=\prod_{i=1}^{m}u_{i}^{b_{i}}-u_{m+1}\,u_{m+2},\\ \partial_{t}u_{i}-d_{i}\Delta u_{i}=-b_{i}\,\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m}u_{i}^{b_{i}}-u_{m+1}\,u_{m+2}\right)\quad\text{ for }\quad i=1,\dots,m.\end{lgathered}\right. (8)

It is complemented with the homogeneous Neumann boundary condition and initial data (7) (for i=1,…,m+2i=1,\dots,m+2).

Then, we can prove the

Theorem 3.

Let d≤4d\leq 4 and Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a smooth (𝒞2\mathscr{C}^{2}) bounded domain. Let di>0d_{i}>0 be constant diffusion rates, and suppose that the initial data uiin≥0u_{i}^{\mathrm{in}}\geq 0 lie in 𝒞2​(Ω¯)\mathscr{C}^{2}(\overline{\Omega}) and are compatible with the homogeneous Neumann boundary condition of (7).

Then there exists a global (defined on ℝ+×Ω\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Omega) strong (that is, all terms appearing in the equation are defined a.e.) solution to system (8), (7).

A key step of our approach is the study of solutions u:=u⁡(t,x)u:=u(t,x) to the equation

∂tu−Δ⁡(μ​u)=f⁡(t,x),\partial_{t}u-\Delta(\mu u)=f(t,x),

where ff is some forcing and μ:=μ⁡(t,x)\mu:=\mu(t,x) are given diffusion coefficients for which we know only a lower and upper bound (rough coefficients). Such an equation can be studied thanks to duality estimates, see [3, 28]. However, we will rather follow [14, 4], and introduce a new unknown w⁡(t,x):=∫s=0tμ⁡(s,x)​u​(s,x)​𝑑sw(t,x):=\int_{s=0}^{t}\mu(s,x)\,u(s,x)\,\mathrm{d}s.

This leads to the independent study of the boundedness and Hölder regularity of solutions w:=w⁡(t,x)w:=w(t,x) to the parabolic equation (with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions)

a⁡(t,x)​∂tw⁡(t,x)−Δ​w​(t,x)=f⁡(t,x)assuming moreover that ∂tw≥0,a(t,x)\partial_{t}w(t,x)-\Delta w(t,x)=f(t,x)\qquad\text{assuming moreover that }\quad\partial_{t}w\geq 0, (9)

where aa is a “rough” coefficient, i.e., we only suppose that

0<a0≤a≤c0​a0<∞,0<a_{0}\leq a\leq c_{0}a_{0}<\infty, (10)

for some constants a0a_{0} and c0≥1c_{0}\geq 1.

For the forcing ff, we assume that it lies in a suitable Lebesgue space.

The studied parabolic equation (9) is a special case of more general parabolic equations in non-divergence form, which write

∂tw−∑i,jai​j​∂i​jw=f.\partial_{t}w-\sum_{i,j}a^{ij}\partial_{ij}w=f. (11)

In this general case, [23] proved a parabolic version of the ABP maximum principle, stating that ‖w‖L∞\|w\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}} can be estimated by ‖f‖L1+d\|f\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1+d}}, where dd is the space dimension.

We also quote the subsequent works [26, 25, 24, 12, 27, 21, 30, 22] and in the related elliptic case [20], where it is shown that Hölder regularity (that is, w∈𝒞αw\in\mathscr{C}^{\alpha} for some α>0\alpha>0) can even be obtained for Equation (11).

We show in this paper that the additional information ∂tw≥0\partial_{t}w\geq 0 allows a direct comparison with the heat equation (see [14] and in a similar matter [4]), allowing to treat all the details related to the (homogeneous Neumann) boundary condition, and to provide explicit constants in the estimates, including a precise and sharp dependency on the forcing term ff.

Our main result for solutions to (9) is the following.

Theorem 4.

We consider a bounded, 𝒞2\mathscr{C}^{2} domain Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}. Set T>0T>0, and p,q∈[1,∞]p,q\in[1,\infty] such that γ:=2−2p−dq>0\gamma:=2-\frac{2}{p}-\frac{d}{q}>0. ‖w‖𝒞α​([0,T]×Ω¯)≤C∗​(‖f+‖Lp​((0,T],Lq​(Ω))+‖win‖Lip)1−α/γ​(‖f‖Lp​((0,T],Lq​(Ω))+‖win‖Lip)α/γ.\|w\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}([0,T]\times{\overline{\Omega}})}\leq C_{*}\left(\|f_{+}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}((0,T];\textnormal{L}^{q}(\Omega))}+\|w_{\mathrm{in}}\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\right)^{1-\alpha/\gamma}\left(\|f\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}((0,T];\textnormal{L}^{q}(\Omega))}+\|w_{\mathrm{in}}\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\right)^{\alpha/\gamma}.

α:=min⁡(ln⁡([1−δ]−1)ln⁡4,γ,12),\alpha:=\min\left(\frac{\ln([1-\delta]^{-1})}{\ln 4},\gamma,\frac{1}{2}\right),

where

δ:=131568​(98​π)−d2​dd2+1​e−d​c0​|Bd​(0,1)|.\delta:={\frac{13}{1568}}\,\left(98\,\pi\,\right)^{-\frac{d}{2}}\,d^{\frac{d}{2}+1}\,\mathrm{e}^{-dc_{0}}\,|B_{d}(0,1)|.
Remark 5.

Note that we obtain the Hölder regularity uniform up to the boundary of the domain, and to arbitrary small times. To treat those small times, we need to assume some regularity of the initial datum. In Theorem 4, we supposed that winw_{\mathrm{in}} has Lipschitz regularity, which is not optimal (but leads to simplified proofs).

Remark 6.

Compared to the ABP maximum principle in which the forcing lies in LpL^{p} with p=1+dp=1+d, Theorem 4 gets us close to the critical estimate when p=qp=q, as we get arbitrary close to the critical exponent p=1+d/2p=1+d/2 for the forcing.

The crucial step in the proof of our main Theorem is the decay of oscillations. Hence we study around a point z0:=(t0,x0)z_{0}:=(t_{0},x_{0}) the parabolic cylinder QRβ(z0)=(t0−βR2,t0]×Bd(x0,R)Q^{\beta}_{R}(z_{0})=(t_{0}-\beta R^{2},t_{0}]\times B_{d}(x_{0},R) where R>0R>0 is a scaling, parameter and β>0\beta>0 is a parameter which will be chosen small later on. The idea to obtain Hölder regularity is to show that the oscillation of ww over a cylinder QR/4β​(z0)Q^{\beta}_{R/4}(z_{0}) is controlled by the oscillation over QRβ​(z0)Q^{\beta}_{R}(z_{0}) with a factor strictly less than one.

The following Proposition shows such a decay where we include a possible boundary with Neumann boundary data (Note that by scaling for Theorem 4 it will only be used for R=1R=1; we state the general case R>0R>0 for possible other applications).

Remark 8.

Note that we only impose a boundary condition on ww along the graph of ϕ\phi. Further note that by taking ϕ≡−R\phi\equiv-R, it also covers the case without boundary.

In the proofs of the applications (Theorem 1 and Theorem 2), we need nonstandard interpolation estimates that we propose to call “one-sided interpolation estimates”. Since they may be of interest for other results, we write them down here as a self-contained Proposition:

Proposition 9.

Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a bounded 𝒞2\mathscr{C}^{2} domain, and assume p,q∈[1,∞)p,q\in[1,\infty) satisfying d2<32​p≤q\frac{d}{2}<\frac{3}{2}p\leq q. Then for any u,w:Ω→ℝu,w:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} such that 0≤u≤Δ​w0\leq u\leq\Delta w in Ω\Omega, it holds that

‖u‖Lq​(Ω)≤Cd,p,q​‖w‖L∞​(Ω)1−2−d/q3−d/p​‖∇u‖Lp​(Ω)2−d/q3−d/p+Cd,p,q​‖w‖L∞​(Ω),\|u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(\Omega)}\leq C_{d,p,q}\,\|{w}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\Omega)}^{1-\frac{2-d/q}{3-d/p}}\,\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(\Omega)}^{\frac{2-d/q}{3-d/p}}+C_{d,p,q}\,\|{w}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\Omega)}, (12)

where Cd,p,q>0C_{d,p,q}>0 is a constant depending only on d,p,qd,p,q.

Moreover, assuming that α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), and that q≥3−α2−α​p>d2−αq\geq\frac{3-\alpha}{2-\alpha}\,p>\frac{d}{2-\alpha}. Then for any u,w:Ω→ℝu,w:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} such that 0≤u≤Δ​w0\leq u\leq\Delta w, it holds that

‖u‖Lq​(Ω)≤Cd,p,q,α​‖w‖𝒞α​(Ω¯)1−2−α−d/q3−α−d/p​‖∇u‖Lp​(Ω)2−α−d/q3−α−d/p+Cd,p,q,α​‖w‖𝒞α​(Ω¯),\|u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(\Omega)}\leq C_{d,p,q,\alpha}\,\|{w}\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})}^{1-\frac{2-\alpha-d/q}{3-\alpha-d/p}}\,\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(\Omega)}^{\frac{2-\alpha-d/q}{3-\alpha-d/p}}+C_{d,p,q,\alpha}\,\|{w}\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})}, (13)

Note that the name “one-sided interpolation estimates” is related to the fact that we assume that 0≤u≤Δ​w0\leq u\leq\Delta w instead of assuming the stronger (and more classical) identity u=Δ​wu=\Delta w.

A study of more general estimates of this form with applications to different equations is in preparation [1].

Section 2 is devoted to the proof of Theorem 4. We start with estimates for the heat equation in Subsection 2.1. Then we use a comparison between the heat equation and the equation with rough coefficients (9), (10), and obtain the decay of oscillation (Proposition 7) in Subsection 2.2. Finally, we perform global bounds to start the iteration and conclude Theorem 4 in Subsection 2.3 by using iteratively Proposition 7. We present the proof of our first application (Theorem 1) in Section 3, and of our second application (Theorem 2 and its extensions, including Theorem 3) in Section 4. The Appendix A contains the proof of the “one-sided interpolation estimates” appearing in Theorem 1.

2 Hölder regularity for heat equation with rough scalar coefficient

2.1 Estimates for the heat kernel

We first establish estimates for the heat kernel, in particular in the case of a domain with boundaries. There is a huge literature on heat kernels in which more advanced estimates in more general settings are presented, see for example [35, 17, 8, 41] and the references therein.

The starting point for our estimates is the extension operator for functions lying in a Sobolev space from a domain towards the whole space. This is a classical topic, see e.g. [2, 13]. We recall a classical estimate for a general domain, and state moreover the basic reflection estimate, pointing out the dependency of the constant on the boundary.

Lemma 10.

Let Ω\Omega be a 𝒞1\mathscr{C}^{1} domain of  ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Then, there exists an extension operator E2:H1​(Ω)↦H1​(ℝd)E_{2}:\textnormal{H}^{1}(\Omega)\mapsto\textnormal{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and a constant CE​(Ω)>0C_{E}(\Omega)>0 depending only on Ω\Omega such that

‖E2​u‖H1​(ℝd)≤CE​(Ω)​‖u‖H1​(Ω).\|E_{2}u\|_{\textnormal{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq C_{E}(\Omega)\,\|u\|_{\textnormal{H}^{1}(\Omega)}.

Moreover, for a 𝒞1\mathscr{C}^{1} function ϕ:ℝd−1↦ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d-1}\mapsto\mathbb{R}, we define the domain

Ω+={(x′,xd)∈ℝd:xd>ϕ⁡(x′)}.\Omega_{+}=\{(x^{\prime},x_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:x_{d}>\phi(x^{\prime})\}.

Then there exists an extension operator E2:H1​(Ω+)↦H1​(ℝd)E_{2}:\textnormal{H}^{1}(\Omega_{+})\mapsto\textnormal{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and L1​(Ω+)↦L1​(ℝd)\textnormal{L}^{1}(\Omega_{+})\mapsto\textnormal{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that

‖E2​u‖H1​(ℝd)≤2​1+‖∇ϕ‖∞2​‖u‖H1​(Ω+).\|E_{2}u\|_{\textnormal{H}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq 2\,\sqrt{1+\|\nabla\phi\|_{\infty}^{2}}\,\,\|u\|_{\textnormal{H}^{1}(\Omega_{+})}.

and

‖E2​u‖L1​(ℝd)≤2​‖u‖L1​(Ω+).\|E_{2}u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq 2\,\|u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}(\Omega_{+})}.
Proof.

The first part of the statement is a classical result, cf. [2]. For the second part, it suffices to define and bound the extension for a smooth function u∈H1​(Ω+)u\in\textnormal{H}^{1}(\Omega_{+}). We define the extended function u¯\bar{u} by reflection as

E2​u​(x′,xd)=u¯​(x′,xd):={u⁡(x′,xd)if ​xd≥ϕ⁡(x′),u⁡(x′,2​ϕ​(x′)−xd)if ​xd<ϕ⁡(x′).E_{2}u(x^{\prime},x_{d})=\bar{u}(x^{\prime},x_{d}):=\begin{cases}u(x^{\prime},x_{d})&\text{if }x_{d}\geq\phi(x^{\prime}),\\ u(x^{\prime},2\phi(x^{\prime})-x_{d})&\text{if }x_{d}<\phi(x^{\prime}).\end{cases}

Then, we directly get ‖u¯‖L1​(ℝd)2≤2​‖u‖L1​(Ω+)2\|\bar{u}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{2}\leq 2\,\|u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}(\Omega_{+})}^{2} and ‖u¯‖L2​(ℝd)2≤2​‖u‖L2​(Ω+)2\|\bar{u}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{2}\leq 2\,\|u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega_{+})}^{2}. Moreover, for xd<ϕ⁡(x′)x_{d}<\phi(x^{\prime}), we find for the derivatives

∇iu¯\displaystyle\nabla_{i}\bar{u} =∇iu|(x′,2​ϕ​(x′)−xd)+2∇iϕ∇du|(x′,2​ϕ​(x′)−xd),i=1,…,d−1\displaystyle=\nabla_{i}u|_{(x^{\prime},2\phi(x^{\prime})-x_{d})}+2\nabla_{i}\phi\,\nabla_{d}u|_{(x^{\prime},2\phi(x^{\prime})-x_{d})},\qquad i=1,\dots,d-1
∇du¯\displaystyle\nabla_{d}\bar{u} =∇du|(x′,2​ϕ​(x′)−xd).\displaystyle=\nabla_{d}u|_{(x^{\prime},2\phi(x^{\prime})-x_{d})}.

This shows that

‖u¯‖L2​(ℝd)2+‖∇u¯‖L2​(ℝd)2≤∫Ω+(2​|u|2+2​|∇du|2+∑i=1d−1[3​|∇iu|2+4​|∇iϕ|2​|∇du|2])​𝑑x≤(4+4​‖∇ϕ‖∞2)​‖u¯‖H1​(Ω+)2,\begin{split}\|\bar{u}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{2}+\|\nabla\bar{u}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{2}&\leq\int_{\Omega_{+}}\bigg(2\,|u|^{2}+2\,|\nabla_{d}u|^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}[3\,|\nabla_{i}u|^{2}+4\,|\nabla_{i}\phi|^{2}\,|\nabla_{d}u|^{2}]\bigg)\,\mathrm{d}x\\ &\leq(4+4\|\nabla\phi\|_{\infty}^{2})\,\|\bar{u}\|_{\textnormal{H}^{1}(\Omega_{+})}^{2},\end{split}

which then yields the statement. ∎

Given a domain Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, we split its boundary into ∂Ωd\partial\Omega_{d} (Dirichlet boundary condition) and ∂Ωn\partial\Omega_{n} (Neumann boundary condition). For the domain with the split boundary, we define for a fixed y∈Ωy\in\Omega the mixed heat kernel ΓΩ\Gamma_{\Omega} as the solution to

{(∂t−Δx)ΓΩ(t,x,y)=0for ​(t,x)∈(0,∞)×Ω,ΓΩ​(t,x,y)=0for ​(t,x)∈(0,T)×∂Ωd,n→⋅∇xΓΩ​(t,x,y)=0for ​(t,x)∈(0,T)×∂Ωn,limt↓0ΓΩ​(t,⋅,y)=δy.\left\{\begin{aligned} &(\partial_{t}-\Delta_{x})\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,x,y)=0&&\text{for }(t,x)\in(0,\infty)\times\Omega,\\ &\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,x,y)=0&&\text{for }(t,x)\in(0,T)\times\partial\Omega_{d},\\ &\vec{n}\cdot\nabla_{x}\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,x,y)=0&&\text{for }(t,x)\in(0,T)\times\partial\Omega_{n},\\ &\lim_{t\downarrow 0}\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,\cdot,y)=\delta_{y}.\end{aligned}\right.

We now develop estimates on ΓΩ\Gamma_{\Omega}.

Lemma 11.

Using the notation above, we suppose that there exists EE an extension operator from the piecewise-𝒞1\mathscr{C}^{1} domain Ω\Omega to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} in H1\textnormal{H}^{1} and L1\textnormal{L}^{1} for functions {u∈H1​(Ω):u|∂Ωd=0}\{u\in\textnormal{H}^{1}(\Omega):u|_{\partial\Omega_{d}}=0\} and set ‖|E|‖=max⁡(‖E‖H1→H1,‖E‖L1→L1)|||E|||=\max(\|E\|_{\textnormal{H}^{1}\to\textnormal{H}^{1}},\|E\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}\to\textnormal{L}^{1}}). Then for any time T>0T>0, there exists a constant CΩ,T,d>0C_{\Omega,T,d}>0 depending on TT, dd, and Ω\Omega through ‖|E|‖|||E||| only (and increasing with respect to TT), such that for all p∈[1,∞)p\in[1,\infty), y∈Ωy\in\Omega and t∈(0,T)t\in(0,T),

∥ΓΩ(t,⋅,y)∥L1​(Ω)≤1,∥ΓΩ(t,⋅,y)∥Lp​(Ω)≤CΩ,T,dt−d/(2p′),∥ΓΩ(t,⋅,y)∥L∞​(Ω)≤CΩ,T,dt−d/2,\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}(\Omega)}\leq 1,\qquad\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(\Omega)}\leq C_{\Omega,T,d}\,t^{-d/(2p^{\prime})},\qquad\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq C_{\Omega,T,d}\,t^{-d/2},

and for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega and t∈(0,T)t\in(0,T),

∥ΓΩ(t,x,⋅)∥L1​(Ω)≤1,∥ΓΩ(t,x,⋅)∥Lp​(Ω)≤CΩ,T,dt−d/(2p′),∥ΓΩ(t,x,⋅)∥L∞​(Ω)≤CΩ,T,dt−d/2.\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,x,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}(\Omega)}\leq 1,\qquad\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,x,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(\Omega)}\leq C_{\Omega,T,d}\,t^{-d/(2p^{\prime})},\qquad\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,x,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq C_{\Omega,T,d}\,t^{-d/2}.
Proof.

By the construction of the heat kernel, we have for all t>0t>0 that ΓΩ≥0\Gamma_{\Omega}\geq 0 (thanks to the minimum principle) and ‖ΓΩ​(t,⋅,y)‖L1​(Ω)≤1\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}(\Omega)}\leq 1 (since n→⋅∇ΓΩ|∂Ωd≤0\vec{n}\cdot\nabla\Gamma_{\Omega}|_{\partial\Omega_{d}}\leq 0, where n→\vec{n} is the outward normal vector at a point of ∂Ω\partial\Omega).

Moreover, we find the dissipation for the evolution of the square of the L2L^{2} norm:

12​dd​t​‖ΓΩ​(t,⋅,y)‖L2​(Ω)2=−‖∇ΓΩ​(t,⋅,y)‖L2​(Ω)2.\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}=-\|\nabla\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}.

The Nash inequality states that there exists a constant CNash,d>0C_{\mathrm{Nash},d}>0 only depending on dd such that for any function vv over ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d},

‖v‖L2​(ℝd)1+2d≤CNash,d​‖∇v‖L2​(ℝd)​‖v‖L1​(ℝd)2d.\|v\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{1+\frac{2}{d}}\leq C_{\mathrm{Nash},d}\,\|\nabla v\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\,\|v\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{\frac{2}{d}}.

Using the extension operator EE, we end up with

‖ΓΩ‖L2​(Ω)1+2d\displaystyle\|\Gamma_{\Omega}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}^{1+\frac{2}{d}} ≤‖E​ΓΩ‖L2​(ℝd)1+2d\displaystyle\leq\|E\Gamma_{\Omega}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{1+\frac{2}{d}}
≤CNash,d​‖∇(E​ΓΩ)‖L2​(ℝd)​‖E​ΓΩ‖L1​(ℝd)2d\displaystyle\leq C_{\mathrm{Nash},d}\,\|\nabla(E\Gamma_{\Omega})\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\,\|E\Gamma_{\Omega}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{\frac{2}{d}}
≤CNash,d​‖|E|‖1+2d​‖ΓΩ‖L2​(Ω)2+‖∇ΓΩ‖L2​(Ω)2​‖ΓΩ‖L1​(Ω)2d,\displaystyle\leq C_{\mathrm{Nash},d}\,|||E|||^{1+\frac{2}{d}}\,\sqrt{\|\Gamma_{\Omega}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}+\|\nabla\Gamma_{\Omega}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}}\,\|\Gamma_{\Omega}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}(\Omega)}^{\frac{2}{d}},

so that, using the estimate ‖ΓΩ​(t,⋅,y)‖L1​(Ω)≤1\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}(\Omega)}\leq 1, we end up with

‖∇ΓΩ‖L2​(Ω)2≥C′′​‖ΓΩ‖L2​(Ω)2+4d−‖ΓΩ‖L2​(Ω)2,\|\nabla\Gamma_{\Omega}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}\geq C^{\prime\prime}\,\|\Gamma_{\Omega}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}^{2+\frac{4}{d}}-\|\Gamma_{\Omega}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}^{2},

with C′′:=CNash,d−2​‖|E|‖−2−4dC^{\prime\prime}:=C_{\mathrm{Nash},d}^{-2}\,|||E|||^{-2-\frac{4}{d}}, and finally

12​dd​t​‖ΓΩ​(t,⋅,y)‖L2​(Ω)2≤−C′′​‖ΓΩ​(t,⋅,y)‖L2​(Ω)2+4d+‖ΓΩ​(t,⋅,y)‖L2​(Ω)2.\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}\leq-C^{\prime\prime}\,\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}^{2+\frac{4}{d}}+\,\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}.

Denoting q⁡(t):=(‖ΓΩ​(t,⋅,y)‖L2​(Ω)2)−2dq(t):=\bigg(\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}\bigg)^{-\frac{2}{d}}, we see therefore that

q′​(t)≥4d​(C′′−q⁡(t)),q^{\prime}(t)\geq\frac{4}{d}\,(C^{\prime\prime}-q(t)),

which implies

q⁡(t)≥C′′​4d​t​e−4d​t,q(t)\geq C^{\prime\prime}\,\frac{4}{d}\,t\,\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{4}{d}\,t},

so that in the end

‖ΓΩ​(t,⋅,y)‖L2​(Ω)2≤(C′′​4d)−d2​e2​T​t−d2.\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}\leq\left(C^{\prime\prime}\,\frac{4}{d}\right)^{-\frac{d}{2}}\,\mathrm{e}^{2T}\,t^{-\frac{d}{2}}.

This yields the claimed L2\textnormal{L}^{2} bound.

For the L∞\textnormal{L}^{\infty} bound, note first that the Laplace operator is self-adjoint, so that ΓΩ​(t,x,y)=ΓΩ​(t,y,x)\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,x,y)=\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,y,x). By the semigroup property, we therefore find that

ΓΩ​(t,x,y)\displaystyle\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,x,y) =∫ΩΓΩ​(t/2,x,z)​ΓΩ​(t/2,z,y)​𝑑z\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\Gamma_{\Omega}(t/2,x,z)\,\Gamma_{\Omega}(t/2,z,y)\,\mathrm{d}z
≤∥ΓΩ(t/2,x,⋅)∥L2​(Ω)∥ΓΩ(t/2,⋅,y)∥L2​(Ω)\displaystyle\leq\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t/2,x,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}\;\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t/2,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}
≤‖ΓΩ​(t/2,⋅,x)‖L2​(Ω)​‖ΓΩ​(t/2,⋅,y)‖L2​(Ω),\displaystyle\leq\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t/2,\cdot,x)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)}\;\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(t/2,\cdot,y)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{2}(\Omega)},

and we use the already established L2\textnormal{L}^{2} bound to conclude.

A direct interpolation between the L1\textnormal{L}^{1} and L∞\textnormal{L}^{\infty} estimates yields the Lp\textnormal{L}^{p} estimate stated in the Lemma. Finally, the self-adjointness argument leads to the second group of estimates. ∎

In the context of the domains appearing in the proof of Proposition 7 (but keeping the notations of Lemma 11), we write down for the related geometry the following statement:

Lemma 12.

Fix T>0T>0. Then there exists a constant CT,d∗C^{*}_{T,d} such that for any domain

Ω:=Bd​(0,R)∩{(x′,xd)∈ℝd:xd>ϕ⁡(x′)}\Omega:=B_{d}(0,R)\cap\{(x^{\prime},x_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:x_{d}>\phi(x^{\prime})\}

for R>0R>0 and ϕ:ℝd−1→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d-1}\to\mathbb{R} with ‖∇ϕ‖∞≤111​d\|\nabla\phi\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{11d} with ∂Ωn=Bd(0,R)∩{x′,xd)∈ℝd:xd=ϕ(x′)}\partial\Omega_{n}=B_{d}(0,R)\cap\{x^{\prime},x_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:x_{d}=\phi(x^{\prime})\} and ∂Ωd=∂Ω∖∂Ωn\partial\Omega_{d}=\partial\Omega\setminus\partial\Omega_{n} the constant CΩ,T,dC_{\Omega,T,d} appearing in Lemma 11 is bounded by CT,d∗C^{*}_{T,d}.

For the domain considered in the statement, we need an extension operator EE for functions f∈H1​(Ω)f\in\textnormal{H}^{1}(\Omega) such that f|∂Ωd=0f|_{\partial\Omega_{d}}=0, for the norms H1\textnormal{H}^{1} and L1\textnormal{L}^{1}.

We can first extend ff to Ω+:={(x′,xd)∈ℝd:xd>ϕ⁡(x′)}\Omega_{+}:=\{(x^{\prime},x_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:x_{d}>\phi(x^{\prime})\} by setting E1​f=0E_{1}f=0 on Ω+∖Ω\Omega_{+}\setminus\Omega, and E1​f=fE_{1}f=f on Ω\Omega. Recalling that f|∂Ωd=0f|_{\partial\Omega_{d}}=0, we see that ‖E1‖H1→H1=1||E_{1}||_{H^{1}\to H^{1}}=1 and ‖E1‖L1→L1=1||E_{1}||_{L^{1}\to L^{1}}=1. We then use Lemma 10 (with Ω\Omega in this lemma corresponding to Ω+\Omega_{+} here) to build the operator E2E_{2} from H1​(Ω+)H^{1}(\Omega_{+}) to H1​(ℝd)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), so that still thanks to Lemma 10, ‖|E2​E1|‖=‖|E2|‖≤2​1+1121​d2|||E_{2}\,E_{1}|||=|||E_{2}|||\leq 2\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{121d^{2}}}, and we conclude the Lemma by setting E:=E2​E1E:=E_{2}\,E_{1}. ∎

We now write down an estimate which is a direct consequence of Lemma 11, and which will be used several times in the sequel.

Lemma 13.

Let Ω\Omega be a piecewise - 𝒞1\mathscr{C}^{1} domain of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and suppose that there exists EE an extension operator from Ω\Omega to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for H1\textnormal{H}^{1} and L1\textnormal{L}^{1} functions. We consider f∈Lp​([0,T],Lq​(Ω))f\in\textnormal{L}^{p}([0,T];\textnormal{L}^{q}(\Omega)), with p,q∈[1,∞]p,q\in[1,\infty] and 2p+dq<2\frac{2}{p}+\frac{d}{q}<2. Then, for t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], x∈Ωx\in\Omega, a>0a>0,

|∫0t∫ΩΓΩ​(t−sa,x,y)​f​(s,y)​𝑑y​𝑑s|≤CΩ,Ta,d​ad2​q​(T1−d2​p′q1−d2​p′q)1p′​‖f‖Lp​([0,T],Lq​(Ω)).\bigg|\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\Omega}\Gamma_{\Omega}(\frac{t-s}{a},x,y)\,f(s,y)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}s\bigg|\leq C_{\Omega,\frac{T}{a},d}\,a^{\frac{d}{2q}}\,\left(\frac{T^{1-\frac{d}{2}\frac{p^{\prime}}{q}}}{1-\frac{d}{2}\frac{p^{\prime}}{q}}\right)^{\frac{1}{p^{\prime}}}\,\|f\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}([0,T];\textnormal{L}^{q}(\Omega))}.
Proof.

We compute

|∫0t∫ΩΓΩ​(t−sa,x,y)​f​(s,y)​𝑑y​𝑑s|≤∫0t∥ΓΩ(t−sa,x,⋅)∥Lq′​(Ω)∥f(s,⋅)∥Lq​(Ω)ds≤CΩ,Ta,d​∫0t(t−sa)−d2​q​‖f⁡(s,⋅)‖Lq​(Ω)​𝑑s≤CΩ,Ta,d​ad2​q​[∫0t(t−s)−d​p′2​q​𝑑s]1p′​(∫0t‖f⁡(s,⋅)‖Lq​(Ω)p​𝑑s)1p≤CΩ,Ta,d​ad2​q​(T1−d2​p′q1−dq​p′2)1p′​‖f‖Lp​([0,T],Lq​(Ω)).∎\begin{split}\bigg|\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\Omega}\Gamma_{\Omega}(\frac{t-s}{a},x,y)\,f(s,y)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}s\bigg|&\leq\int_{0}^{t}\|\Gamma_{\Omega}(\frac{t-s}{a},x,\cdot)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q^{\prime}}(\Omega)}\,\|f(s,\cdot\,)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(\Omega)}\,\mathrm{d}s\\ &\leq C_{\Omega,\frac{T}{a},d}\int_{0}^{t}\left(\frac{t-s}{a}\right)^{-\frac{d}{2q}}\,\|f(s,\cdot\,)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(\Omega)}\,\mathrm{d}s\\ &\leq C_{\Omega,\frac{T}{a},d}\,a^{\frac{d}{2q}}\,\bigg[\int_{0}^{t}({t-s})^{-\frac{dp^{\prime}}{2q}}\,\mathrm{d}s\bigg]^{\frac{1}{p^{\prime}}}\,\bigg(\int_{0}^{t}\,\|f(s,\cdot\,)\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(\Omega)}^{p}\,\mathrm{d}s\bigg)^{\frac{1}{p}}\\ &\leq C_{\Omega,\frac{T}{a},d}\,a^{\frac{d}{2q}}\,\left(\frac{T^{1-\frac{d}{2}\frac{p^{\prime}}{q}}}{1-\frac{d}{q}\frac{p^{\prime}}{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{p^{\prime}}}\,\|f\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}([0,T];\textnormal{L}^{q}(\Omega))}.\qed\end{split}

For treating small times, we will also need the following moment bound.

Lemma 14.

Assume the setup of Lemma 11. For 1/2>ϵ>01/2>\epsilon>0, there exists a constant C~ϵ,T>0\tilde{C}_{\epsilon,T}>0 depending on ϵ\epsilon, TT, dd and Ω\Omega only through |Ω||\Omega| and ‖|E|‖|||E|||, and increasing with respect to TT, such that when t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] and y∈Ωy\in\Omega,

m⁡(t,y):=∫Ω|x−y|​ΓΩ​(t,x,y)​𝑑x≤C~ϵ,T​t12−ϵ.m(t,y):=\int_{\Omega}|x-y|\,\Gamma_{\Omega}(t,x,y)\,\mathrm{d}x\leq\tilde{C}_{\epsilon,T}\,t^{\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon}.

Using a more careful argument as in [32] allows to remove the ϵ\epsilon in the inequality above.

Proof.

since

∫∂Ωd∪∂Ωn(ΓΩ1+ΓΩ+ln(1+ΓΩ))∇ΓΩ⋅n→(x)dσ(x)=0.\int_{\partial\Omega_{d}\cup\partial\Omega_{n}}\left(\frac{\Gamma_{\Omega}}{1+\Gamma_{\Omega}}+\ln(1+\Gamma_{\Omega})\right)\,\nabla\Gamma_{\Omega}\cdot\vec{n}(x)\,\mathrm{d}\sigma(x)=0.

so that (changing the definition of C~ϵ,T\tilde{C}_{\epsilon,T}),

2.2 Decay of oscillations

For the decay of oscillation, we obtain a new domain UU by cutting out a ball. This reduced domain can have a part ∂Un\partial U_{n} from the original domain where we still have the Neumann boundary data. We then have a subdomain UrU_{r} on which we want to obtain a reduced oscillation. Note that this subdomain typically can hit or be close to the boundary part ∂U\partial U. For the reduction of the oscillation, we consider a further subdomain UeU_{e} for which we assume that the heat kernel starting from UeU_{e} is strictly positive in UrU_{r} after a suitable time with a uniform bound.

In this general setting, we formulate an abstract lemma for the decay of oscillation.

3 Global strong solutions to the triangular SKT system in dimension 3 and 4

In this section, we present the proof of Theorem 1.

We first state the most basic a priori estimate for system (1) – (5), considering (sufficiently smooth) solutions u,v≥0u,v\geq 0 of the system.

From the maximum principle applied to the second equation, we get from the start that (for any T>0T>0), ‖v‖L∞​([0,T]×Ω)≤C\|v\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}([0,T]\times\Omega)}\leq C. We denote here and in the sequel by CC a constant depending only on Ω\Omega, TT, the initial data and the parameters of the system (we will denote by CpC_{p} a constant when it also depends on an extra parameter pp).

Integrating the first equation on Ω\Omega, we also see that ‖u‖L∞​([0,T],L1​(Ω))≤C\|u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}([0,T];\textnormal{L}^{1}(\Omega))}\leq C.

Then, using upu^{p} with p>0p>0 as a multiplier in the first equation, we get

dd​t∫Ωup+1p+1+p∫Ωup−1∇u⋅((d1+σv)∇u+σu∇v)=∫Ωup+1(ru−d11u−d12v),\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_{\Omega}\frac{u^{p+1}}{p+1}+p\int_{\Omega}u^{p-1}\nabla u\cdot\left((d_{1}+\sigma\,v)\nabla u+\sigma u\,\nabla v\right)=\int_{\Omega}u^{p+1}\,(r_{u}-d_{11}\,u-d_{12}\,v),

so that

dd​t∫Ωup+1p+1+p∫Ω(d1+σv)up−1|∇u|2+σ∫Ωup∇u⋅∇v=∫Ωup+1(ru−d11u−d12v),\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_{\Omega}\frac{u^{p+1}}{p+1}+p\int_{\Omega}(d_{1}+\sigma\,v)u^{p-1}|\nabla u|^{2}+\sigma\int_{\Omega}u^{p}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v=\int_{\Omega}u^{p+1}\,(r_{u}-d_{11}\,u-d_{12}\,v),

and (using Young’s inequality)

dd​t​∫Ωup+1p+1+d1​4​p(p+1)2​∫Ω|∇(up+12)|2≤Cp+Cp​∫Ωup+1​|Δ​v|.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_{\Omega}\frac{u^{p+1}}{p+1}+d_{1}\,\frac{4p}{(p+1)^{2}}\,\int_{\Omega}\,|\nabla(u^{\frac{p+1}{2}})|^{2}\leq C_{p}+C_{p}\int_{\Omega}u^{p+1}\,|\Delta v|.

Using maximal regularity in the equation for vv (and again Young’s inequality), we get

∫Ωup+1p+1​(T)+d1​4​p(p+1)2​∫0T∫Ω|∇(up+12)|2≤Cp+Cp​∫0T∫Ωup+2.\int_{\Omega}\frac{u^{p+1}}{p+1}(T)+d_{1}\,\frac{4p}{(p+1)^{2}}\,\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}\,|\nabla(u^{\frac{p+1}{2}})|^{2}\leq C_{p}+C_{p}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Omega}u^{p+2}. (31)

Proceeding as in [9], we see that if uu is bounded in Lp+2​([0,T]×Ω)\textnormal{L}^{p+2}([0,T]\times\Omega), then u∈L∞​([0,T],Lp+1​(Ω))u\in\textnormal{L}^{\infty}([0,T];\textnormal{L}^{p+1}(\Omega)) and ∇(up+12)∈L2​([0,T]×Ω)\nabla(u^{\frac{p+1}{2}})\in\textnormal{L}^{2}([0,T]\times\Omega), so that after using a Sobolev embedding, an interpolation and an induction procedure, we get that u∈L∞([0,T];∩p∈[1,∞)Lp(Ω))u\in\textnormal{L}^{\infty}([0,T];\cap_{p\in[1,\infty)}\textnormal{L}^{p}(\Omega)) as soon as uu is bounded in Lq​([0,T]×Ω)\textnormal{L}^{q}([0,T]\times\Omega) for some q>1+d2q>1+\frac{d}{2}.

Thanks to the improved duality lemma of [3], we know that (denoting Lr+0:=∪s>0Lr+s\textnormal{L}^{r+0}:=\cup_{s>0}\textnormal{L}^{r+s} here and in the rest of the proof)

u∈L2+0​([0,T]×Ω),u\in\textnormal{L}^{2+0}([0,T]\times\Omega), (32)

(cf. [9]), so that we get that uu is bounded in L∞([0,T];∩p∈[1,∞)Lp(Ω))\textnormal{L}^{\infty}([0,T];\cap_{p\in[1,\infty)}\textnormal{L}^{p}(\Omega)) in the case when d=1d=1 or d=2d=2. Standard arguments involving an approximation procedure or a continuation result (cf. [9]) yield the result of Theorem 1 in that case. See also [29] for a slightly different approach for the same result.

In order to treat the case of dimension d=3d=3 (and d=4d=4), we now provide new arguments. We introduce the quantity m:=m⁡(t,x)m:=m(t,x) defined as the solution of the heat equation

∂tm−Δ​m=u⁡(d11​u+d12​v),\partial_{t}m-\Delta m=u\,(d_{11}u+d_{12}v),

together with the (homogeneous) Neumann boundary condition ∇m⋅n→​(x)=0\nabla m\cdot\vec{n}(x)=0 on [0,T]×∂Ω[0,T]\times\partial\Omega, and the initial datum m⁡(0,⋅)=0m(0,\cdot)=0. By the minimum principle, it is clear that m≥0m\geq 0.

Defining ν:=μ​u+mu+m\nu:=\frac{\mu\,u+m}{u+m}, we observe that min⁡(1,d1)≤ν≤max⁡(1,d1+σ​‖v‖∞)\min(1,d_{1})\leq\nu\leq\max(1,d_{1}+\sigma\,\|v\|_{\infty}), and u+mu+m satisfies the equation

∂t(u+m)−Δ⁡(ν⁡(u+m))=ru​u,\partial_{t}(u+m)-\Delta(\nu\,(u+m))=r_{u}\,u,

together with the (homogeneous) Neumann boundary condition ∇(μ​u+m)⋅n→​(x)=0\nabla(\mu\,u+m)\cdot\vec{n}(x)=0 on [0,T]×∂Ω[0,T]\times\partial\Omega, and the initial condition (u+m)​(0,x)≡uin​(x)(u+m)(0,x)\equiv u_{\mathrm{in}}(x). As a consequence, the improved duality lemma of [3] ensures that

u,m∈L2+0​([0,T]×Ω),u,m\in\textnormal{L}^{2+0}([0,T]\times\Omega), (33)

where (here and in the sequel) we use the shorthand Lp+0:=∪q>pLqL^{p+0}:=\cup_{q>p}L^{q}.

We now consider the quantity w:=∫0t(μ​u+m)w:=\int_{0}^{t}(\mu u+m), and observe that w≥0w\geq 0 and ∂tw≥0\partial_{t}w\geq 0. Moreover Δ​w=∫0tΔ⁡(μ​u+m)=∫0t[∂t(u+m)−ru​u]=u+m−ui​n−ru​∫0tu\Delta w=\int_{0}^{t}\Delta(\mu u+m)=\int_{0}^{t}[\partial_{t}(u+m)-r_{u}\,u]=u+m-u_{in}-r_{u}\,\int_{0}^{t}u.

It satisfies therefore the parabolic equation

ν−1​∂tw−Δ​w=uin+ru​∫0tu,\nu^{-1}\,\partial_{t}w-\Delta w=u_{\mathrm{in}}+r_{u}\,\int_{0}^{t}u, (34)

together with the homogeneous Neumann boundary condition, and the initial condition w⁡(0,⋅)=0w(0,\cdot)=0.

4 Global strong solutions to reaction-diffusion systems in dimension 3 and 4

In this section we present results for reaction-diffusion systems which can be obtained thanks to Theorem 4.

4.1 A simple proof for the existence of global strong solutions to a quadratic reaction-diffusion system

We start with a very short proof of Theorem 2.

Proof.

We observe that when p>0p>0, (sufficiently smooth) solutions of system (6), (7) satisfy the identity

4.2 General dissipative systems with quadratic intermediate sums

In this subsection, we considerably generalise the result of Subsection 4.1, and prove Theorem 3.

We consider reaction-diffusion systems which write

∂tui−diΔui=fi(u1,…,um),i=1,…,m,\partial_{t}u_{i}-d_{i}\Delta u_{i}=f_{i}(u_{1},\dots,u_{m}),\qquad i=1,\dots,m, (50)

together with the Neumann boundary condition and initial condition

∇ui⋅n=0 on [0,T]×∂Ω,ui(0,⋅)=uiini=1,…,m,\nabla u_{i}\cdot n=0\quad{\hbox{ on }}[0,T]\times\partial\Omega,\qquad u_{i}(0,\cdot)=u^{\mathrm{in}}_{i}\qquad i=1,\dots,m, (51)

and introduce the general set of conditions:

  1. (A1)

    (Local Lipschitz and quasi-positivity) The functions fi:ℝm→ℝf_{i}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R} are locally Lipschitz-continuous and satisfy the quasi-positivity condition, for i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m,

    fi​(u1,…,um)≥0 when ui=0 and uj≥0​ for ​j≠i;f_{i}(u_{1},\dots,u_{m})\geq 0\qquad{\hbox{ when }}\qquad u_{i}=0\quad{\hbox{ and }}\quad u_{j}\geq 0{\hbox{ for }}j\neq i;
  2. (A2)

    (Mass dissipation) There exist β1,…,βm>0\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{m}>0 such that for any u1,…,um≥0u_{1},\dots,u_{m}\geq 0,

    ∑i=1mβi​fi​(u1,…,um)≤0;\sum_{i=1}^{m}\beta_{i}\,f_{i}(u_{1},\dots,u_{m})\leq 0;
  3. (A3)

    (Quadratic intermediate sums) There exists a m×mm\times m lower-triangular matrix A=(ai​j)i,j=1,…,mA=(a_{ij})_{i,j=1,\dots,m} with nonnegative elements ai​j≥0a_{ij}\geq 0 and strictly positive diagonal coefficients ai​i>0a_{ii}>0 (so that AA is invertible), and K>0K>0 such that for i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m it holds that

    ∑j=1iai​j​fj​(u1,…,um)≤K​(1+∑i=1mui)2​ for ​ui≥0.\sum_{j=1}^{i}a_{ij}\,f_{j}(u_{1},\dots,u_{m})\leq K\Big(1+\sum_{i=1}^{m}u_{i}\Big)^{2}{\hbox{ for }}u_{i}\geq 0.

Those conditions are used in the following

Proposition 19.

Let Ω\Omega be a smooth bounded open subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with dimension d≤4d\leq 4. Further consider coefficients di>0d_{i}>0 for i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m, and reaction functions fi:ℝm→ℝf_{i}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R} satisfying conditions (A1), (A2) and (A3). We also assume that uiin≥0u^{\mathrm{in}}_{i}\geq 0 lies in 𝒞2​(Ω¯)\mathscr{C}^{2}(\overline{\Omega}) and is compatible with the Neumann boundary condition, for i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m.

Then there exists a global (defined on ℝ+×Ω\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Omega) and strong (all terms are defined a.e.) solution to system (50), (51).

We refer to [14] for detailed references on the history of general problems using the same kind of assumptions. Under assumptions close to (A1), (A2) and the extra assumption |fj(u1,..,um)|≤K(1+∑i=1mui)2+η|f_{j}(u_{1},..,u_{m})|\leq K\Big(1+\sum_{i=1}^{m}u_{i}\Big)^{2+\eta} with η>0\eta>0 small, existence of a unique global classical solution to (50) is shown in [14, 15], together with uniformity in large time of the L∞\textnormal{L}^{\infty} bounds.

With assumptions close to (A1), (A2), (A3), the evolution (50) is considered in dimension d=1d=1 in [42, 38], and in that case it is even possible to allow for a cubic (or slightly more than cubic) intermediate sum condition. Uniformity in large time of the L∞\textnormal{L}^{\infty} bounds is also provided. In [31], global existence of strong solutions to (50) is obtained in dimension d=2d=2 for assumptions close to (A1), (A2), (A3) together with uniformity in large time of the L∞\textnormal{L}^{\infty} bounds.

Note that in comparison with the hypothesis fj​(u1,…,um)≤K​(1+∑i=1mui)2f_{j}(u_{1},\dots,u_{m})\leq K\Big(1+\sum_{i=1}^{m}u_{i}\Big)^{2}, hypothesis (A3) is more general and allows to consider a variety of chemical reaction in dimension d=3d=3 and d=4d=4. We give some examples of such applications.

Remark 20.

Similar to the slightly superquadratic growth of the reaction term in [14], an inspection of the proof shows that we can allow a slightly superquadratic growth in (A3), i.e. we can allow

∑j=1iai​j​fj​(u1,…,um)≤K​(1+∑i=1mui)2+η​ for ​ui≥0,\sum_{j=1}^{i}a_{ij}\,f_{j}(u_{1},\dots,u_{m})\leq K\Big(1+\sum_{i=1}^{m}u_{i}\Big)^{2+\eta}{\hbox{ for }}u_{i}\geq 0,

for some small η\eta (depending on the different diffusion constants).

Proof.

Among systems satisfying the assumptions of Proposition 19, we exhibit the following ones.

First, we recall system (8) introduced in the introduction, coming out from the reversible chemical reaction b1​S1+⋯+bm​Sm⇌Sm+1+Sm+2b_{1}S_{1}+\dots+b_{m}S_{m}\rightleftharpoons S_{m+1}+S_{m+2} where, m∈ℕ∖{0}m\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\} and for i∈1,…,mi\in 1,\dots,m, we have bi∈ℕ∖{0}b_{i}\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}. {∂tum+1−dm+1​Δ​um+1=∏i=1muibi−um+1​um+2,∂tum+2−dm+2​Δ​um+2=∏i=1muibi−um+1​um+2,∂tui−di​Δ​ui=−bi​(∏i=1muibi−um+1​um+2) for i=1,…,m.\left\{\begin{lgathered}\partial_{t}u_{m+1}-d_{m+1}\Delta u_{m+1}=\prod_{i=1}^{m}u_{i}^{b_{i}}-u_{m+1}\,u_{m+2},\\ \partial_{t}u_{m+2}-d_{m+2}\Delta u_{m+2}=\prod_{i=1}^{m}u_{i}^{b_{i}}-u_{m+1}\,u_{m+2},\\ \partial_{t}u_{i}-d_{i}\Delta u_{i}=-b_{i}\,(\prod_{i=1}^{m}u_{i}^{b_{i}}-u_{m+1}\,u_{m+2})\quad\text{ for }\quad i=1,\dots,m.\end{lgathered}\right. We can also extract some systems from [31], which have a structure close to the previous system, and extend existence of global strong solutions to dimension d=3d=3 and d=4d=4 for those systems.

We first write down such a system, coming out from the reversible chemical reaction S1+2​S2⇌S2+S3S_{1}+2S_{2}\rightleftharpoons S_{2}+S_{3}, which writes

{∂tu1−d1​Δ​u1=u2​u3−u1​u22,∂tu2−d2​Δ​u2=u2​u3−u1​u22,∂tu3−d3​Δ​u3=−(u2​u3−u1​u22).\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}u_{1}-d_{1}\Delta u_{1}=u_{2}\,u_{3}-u_{1}\,u_{2}^{2},\\ \partial_{t}u_{2}-d_{2}\Delta u_{2}=u_{2}\,u_{3}-u_{1}\,u_{2}^{2},\\ \partial_{t}u_{3}-d_{3}\Delta u_{3}=-\,(u_{2}\,u_{3}-u_{1}\,u_{2}^{2}).\end{array}\right. (64)

We see that assumption (A2) holds with β1=β2=1\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=1 and β3=2\beta_{3}=2, while assumption (A3) holds with

A:=(100010112).A:=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 1&1&2\end{array}\right). (65)

For the systems described above, Proposition 19 enables (as in the proof of Theorem 3) to get global strong solutions in dimension d=3d=3 and d=4d=4 for all diffusion rates di>0d_{i}>0, whereas such solutions were built only in dimension d=1d=1 or d=2d=2, or in higher dimension for diffusion rates satisfying constraints, in [31]. Note however that the conditions on the initial data considered in Proposition 19 are significantly more stringent than those of [31]. Finally, we indicate that existence of global strong solutions for superquadratic systems in high dimension is not always possible, since very interesting examples of blowups exist, cf. [33, 34].

Appendix A Proof of the one-sided interpolation estimates

In this section, we present a proof of Proposition 9, which consists of the interpolation inequalities (12) and (13). Those interpolations are used in order to obtain inequality (36).

We first capture the geometry by the Lemma below.

Lemma 21.

Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a bounded 𝒞2\mathscr{C}^{2} domain. Then there exists R0>0R_{0}>0 such that for any 0<R≤R00<R\leq R_{0} and any x0∈Ωx_{0}\in\Omega, there exists x^0∈Ω\hat{x}_{0}\in\Omega such that Bd​(x^0,R/4)⊂ΩB_{d}(\hat{x}_{0},R/4)\subset\Omega and Bd​(x0,R)∩ΩB_{d}(x_{0},R)\cap\Omega is star-shaped with core Bd​(x^0,R/4)B_{d}(\hat{x}_{0},R/4).

Proof.

Like in the proof of Theorem 4, we use that the 𝒞2\mathscr{C}^{2} regularity of the domain implies that for a small enough R0R_{0}, the boundary can be described by a graph corresponding to a function with arbitrary small gradient. In this setting, the claimed point x^0\hat{x}_{0} can always be found. ∎

The next building block of the proof is the following Lemma.

Lemma 22.

Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a bounded 𝒞2\mathscr{C}^{2} domain and R0>0R_{0}>0 obtained from Lemma 21. Then for any x0∈Ωx_{0}\in\Omega and 0<R≤R00<R\leq R_{0}, in the cut ball B:=Bd​(x0,R)∩ΩB:=B_{d}(x_{0},R)\cap\Omega, any functions u:B→ℝ+u:B\to\mathbb{R}^{+}, w:B→ℝw:B\to\mathbb{R} satisfying u≤Δ​wu\leq\Delta w in BB can for any p,q∈[1,∞)p,q\in[1,\infty) be estimated as

‖u‖Lq​(B)≤Cd,p,q​[R1−d⁡(1p−1q)​‖∇u‖Lp​(B)+R−2+dq​‖w‖L∞​(B)],\|u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(B)}\leq C_{d,p,q}\,\bigg[R^{1-d\left(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}\right)}\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B)}+R^{-2+\frac{d}{q}}\|w\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(B)}\,\bigg], (68)

where Cd,p,q>0C_{d,p,q}>0 is a constant depending only on d,p,qd,p,q.

In the same way, for any α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1),

‖u‖Lq​(B)≤Cd,p,q,α​[R1−d⁡(1p−1q)​‖∇u‖Lp​(B)+R−2+α+dq​‖w‖𝒞α​(B¯)],\|u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(B)}\leq C_{d,p,q,\alpha}\,\bigg[R^{1-d\left(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}\right)}\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B)}+R^{-2+\alpha+\frac{d}{q}}\|w\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{B})}\,\bigg], (69)

where Cd,p,q,α>0C_{d,p,q,\alpha}>0 is a constant depending only on d,p,q,αd,p,q,\alpha.

Proof.

We consider a smooth weight function χ:ℝd→ℝ+\chi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{+} such that supp⁡χ⊂Bd​(0,1/4)\supp\chi\subset B_{d}(0,1/4) and ∫χ=1\int\chi=1, and its scaled version

χR​(x)=R−d​χ​(x/R),\chi_{R}(x)=R^{-d}\chi(x/R),

so that supp⁡χR⊂Bd​(0,R/4)\supp\chi_{R}\subset B_{d}(0,R/4) and ∫χR=1\int\chi_{R}=1.

Given x0∈Ωx_{0}\in\Omega and 0<R≤R00<R\leq R_{0}, we consider some x^0\hat{x}_{0} given by Lemma 21 and define the average

u¯:=∫x∈Bd​(0,R/4)u⁡(x^0−x)​χR​(x)​𝑑x.\bar{u}:=\int_{x\in B_{d}(0,R/4)}u(\hat{x}_{0}-x)\,\chi_{R}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.

We then estimate the Lq\textnormal{L}^{q} norm of uu as

‖u‖Lq​(B)≤‖u−u¯‖Lq​(B)+‖u¯‖Lq​(B).\|u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(B)}\leq\|u-\bar{u}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(B)}+\|\bar{u}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(B)}.

For the second term, we estimate (with cdc_{d} the volume of Bd​(0,1)B_{d}(0,1))

‖u¯‖Lq​(B)q\displaystyle\|\bar{u}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(B)}^{q} =|B|​|u¯|q≤cd​Rd​(∫χR​(x)​u​(x^0−x)​𝑑x)q\displaystyle=|B|\,|\bar{u}|^{q}\leq c_{d}\,R^{d}\,\bigg(\int\chi_{R}(x)\,u(\hat{x}_{0}-x)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\bigg)^{q} (70)
≤cd​Rd​(∫χR​(x)​Δ​w​(x^0−x)​𝑑x)q≤cd​Rd​(∫Δ​χR​(x)​w​(x^0−x)​𝑑x)q\displaystyle\leq c_{d}\,R^{d}\,\bigg(\int\chi_{R}(x)\,\Delta w(\hat{x}_{0}-x)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\bigg)^{q}\leq c_{d}\,R^{d}\,\bigg(\int\Delta\chi_{R}(x)\,w(\hat{x}_{0}-x)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\bigg)^{q}
≤cd​Rd​(R−d−2​∫Δ​χ​(xR)​w​(x^0−x)​dx)q≤cd​Rd−2​q​‖Δ​χ‖L1​(ℝd)q​‖w‖L∞​(B)q.\displaystyle\leq c_{d}\,R^{d}\,\bigg(R^{-d-2}\int\Delta\chi(\frac{x}{R})\,w(\hat{x}_{0}-x)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\bigg)^{q}\leq c_{d}\,R^{d-2q}\,\|\Delta\chi\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{q}\,\|w\|_{\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(B)}^{q}.

For the Hölder regularity, the estimate can be changed as

‖u¯‖Lq​(B)q\displaystyle\|\bar{u}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(B)}^{q} ≤cd​Rd​(∫Bd​(0,R/4)Δ​χR​(x)​w​(x^0−x)​𝑑x)q\displaystyle\leq c_{d}\,R^{d}\,\bigg(\int_{B_{d}(0,R/4)}\Delta\chi_{R}(x)\,w(\hat{x}_{0}-x)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\bigg)^{q} (71)
≤cd​Rd​(∫Bd​(0,R/4)Δ​χR​(x)​[w⁡(x^0−x)−|Bd​(0,R/4)|−1​∫Bd​(0,R/4)w⁡(x^0−y)​𝑑y]​𝑑x)q\displaystyle\leq c_{d}\,R^{d}\,\bigg(\int_{B_{d}(0,R/4)}\Delta\chi_{R}(x)\,\bigg[w(\hat{x}_{0}-x)-|B_{d}(0,R/4)|^{-1}\int_{B_{d}(0,R/4)}w(\hat{x}_{0}-y)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\bigg]\,\mathrm{d}x\,\bigg)^{q}
=2−q​cd​Rd​(|Bd​(0,R/4)|−1​∫Bd​(0,R/4)∫Bd​(0,R/4)|x−y|α​[Δ​χR​(x)−Δ​χR​(y)]​w⁡(x^0−x)−w⁡(x^0−y)|x−y|α​𝑑x​𝑑y)q\displaystyle=2^{-q}\,c_{d}\,R^{d}\,\bigg(|B_{d}(0,R/4)|^{-1}\,\int_{B_{d}(0,R/4)}\int_{B_{d}(0,R/4)}|x-y|^{\alpha}\,[\Delta\chi_{R}(x)-\Delta\chi_{R}(y)]\,\frac{w(\hat{x}_{0}-x)-w(\hat{x}_{0}-y)}{|x-y|^{\alpha}}\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\,\bigg)^{q}
≤2q​(cd​Rd)1−q​‖w‖𝒞α​(B¯)q​(R−2−d​∫Bd​(0,R/4)∫Bd​(0,R/4)|x−y|α​|Δ​χ​(xR)−Δ​χ​(yR)|​𝑑x​𝑑y)q\displaystyle\leq 2^{q}(c_{d}\,R^{d})^{1-q}\,\|w\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{B})}^{q}\,\bigg(\,R^{-2-d}\int_{B_{d}(0,R/4)}\int_{B_{d}(0,R/4)}|x-y|^{\alpha}\,\bigg|\Delta\chi(\frac{x}{R})-\Delta\chi(\frac{y}{R})\,\bigg|\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\,\bigg)^{q}
=2q​cd1−q​Rd−(2−α)​q​‖w‖𝒞α​(B¯)q​(∫∫⁡|ξ−η|α​|Δ​χ​(ξ)−Δ​χ​(η)|​dξ​dη)q.\displaystyle=2^{q}\,c_{d}^{1-q}\,R^{d-(2-\alpha)q}\,\|w\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{B})}^{q}\,\bigg(\,\int\int|\xi-\eta|^{\alpha}\,\bigg|\Delta\chi(\xi)-\Delta\chi(\eta)\,\bigg|\,\mathrm{d}\xi\,\mathrm{d}\eta\,\bigg)^{q}.

Note that here, the quantities ‖Δ​χ‖L1​(ℝd)\|\Delta\chi\|_{\textnormal{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})} and ∫∫⁡|ξ−η|α​|Δ​χ​(ξ)−Δ​χ​(η)|​𝑑ξ​𝑑η\int\int|\xi-\eta|^{\alpha}\,\bigg|\Delta\chi(\xi)-\Delta\chi(\eta)\,\bigg|\,\mathrm{d}\xi\,\mathrm{d}\eta are just dimensional constants.

For the first term, we use a Poincaré-Sobolev inequality, that we prove thanks to elementary computations. We first observe that for x∈Bx\in B,

u⁡(x)−u¯=∫[u⁡(x)−u⁡(y)]​χR​(x^0−y)​𝑑y=∫∫s=01∇u​(x+s⁡(y−x))⋅(x−y)​χR​(x^0−y)​𝑑s​𝑑y,u(x)-\bar{u}=\int[u(x)-u(y)]\,\chi_{R}(\hat{x}_{0}-y)\,\mathrm{d}y=\int\int_{s=0}^{1}\nabla u(x+s(y-x))\cdot(x-y)\,\chi_{R}(\hat{x}_{0}-y)\,\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{d}y,

where we use the fundamental theorem of calculus and the fact that BB is star-shaped with the core Bd​(x^0,R/4)B_{d}(\hat{x}_{0},R/4). Hence, using the change of variable z:=s⁡(y−x)z:=s\,(y-x),

|u⁡(x)−u¯|\displaystyle|u(x)-\bar{u}| ≤∫x+z∈B∫s=01|∇u​(x+z)|​|z|s​|χR​(x^0−x−zs)|​d​ssd​𝑑z\displaystyle\leq\int_{x+z\in B}\int_{s=0}^{1}|\nabla u(x+z)|\frac{|z|}{s}\,\left|\chi_{R}\left(\hat{x}_{0}-x-\frac{z}{s}\right)\right|\,\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{s^{d}}\,\mathrm{d}z
≤R−d∥χ∥∞∫x+z∈B|∇u(x+z)||z|∫s=01𝟙{|z|s≤|x^0−x|+R}d​ssd+1dz\displaystyle\leq R^{-d}\|\chi\|_{\infty}\int_{x+z\in B}|\nabla u(x+z)|\,|z|\int_{s=0}^{1}\mathbb{1}_{\{\frac{|z|}{s}\leq|\hat{x}_{0}-x|+R\}}\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{s^{d+1}}\,\mathrm{d}z
≤R−d∥χ∥∞∫x+z∈B𝟙{|z|≤2R}|∇u(x+z)||z|∫s=|z|3​R1d​ssd+1dz\displaystyle\leq R^{-d}\|\chi\|_{\infty}\int_{x+z\in B}\mathbb{1}_{\{|z|\leq 2R\}}|\nabla u(x+z)|\,|z|\,\int_{s=\frac{|z|}{3R}}^{1}\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{s^{d+1}}\,\mathrm{d}z
≤3dd∥χ∥∞∫x+z∈B|∇u(x+z)||z|1−d 1{|z|≤2R}dz,\displaystyle\leq\frac{3^{d}}{d}\,\|\chi\|_{\infty}\,\int_{x+z\in B}|\nabla u(x+z)|\,|z|^{1-d}\,\mathbb{1}_{\{|z|\leq 2R\}}\,\mathrm{d}z,

so that using Young’s inequality for convolutions, we end up, when 1q+1=1p+1r\frac{1}{q}+1=\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{r}, with

‖u−u¯‖Lq​(B)\displaystyle\|u-\bar{u}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(B)} ≤3dd∥∇u∥Lp​(B)∥z↦|z|1−d𝟙|z|≤2​R∥Lr​(ℝd)\displaystyle\leq\frac{3^{d}}{d}\,\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B)}\;\;\|z\mapsto|z|^{1-d}\mathbb{1}_{|z|\leq 2R}\|_{\textnormal{L}^{r}(\mathbb{R}^{d})} (72)
≤Cd,p,q​R1−d⁡(1p−1q)​‖∇u‖Lp​(B).\displaystyle\leq C_{d,p,q}\,R^{1-d\left(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}\right)}\,\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B)}.

The statement of the Lemma is obtained by putting together estimates (70) and (72). ∎

We write down a final Lemma before concluding the proof of Proposition 9.

Lemma 23 (Covering).

Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a bounded 𝒞2\mathscr{C}^{2} domain and R0>0R_{0}>0 obtained by Lemma 21. There exists a constant cd>0c_{d}>0 depending only on the dimension dd such that for every A∈(0,∞)A\in(0,\infty), α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1) and u∈Wl​o​c1,p​(Ω)u\in\textnormal{W}^{1,p}_{loc}(\Omega) for p>d3−αp>\frac{d}{3-\alpha}, there exists a cover ℬ\mathcal{B} of balls BB of Ω\Omega satisfying the following properties:

  • •

    for every B=Bd​(x0,R)∈ℬB=B_{d}(x_{0},R)\in\mathcal{B}, we have that R≤R0R\leq R_{0}.

    Moreover, if R=R0R=R_{0}, it holds that

    ‖∇u‖Lp​(B∩Ω)≤A​R−3+α+dp,\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B\cap\Omega)}\leq A\,R^{-3+\alpha+\frac{d}{p}},

    and, if R<R0R<R_{0}, it holds that

    ‖∇u‖Lp​(B∩Ω)=A​R−3+α+dp.\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B\cap\Omega)}=A\,R^{-3+\alpha+\frac{d}{p}}.
  • •

    every point of Ω\Omega is covered by at most cdc_{d} balls.

Proof.

For a point x∈Ωx\in\Omega, we consider the function R↦R3−α−dp​‖∇u‖Lp​(Bd​(x,R)∩Ω)R\mapsto R^{3-\alpha-\frac{d}{p}}\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B_{d}(x,R)\cap\Omega)}. This function starts for R=0R=0 at zero, and is increasing. Hence either ‖∇u‖Lp​(Bd​(x,R0)∩Ω)≤A​R0−3+α+dp\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B_{d}(x,R_{0})\cap\Omega)}\leq A\,R_{0}^{-3+\alpha+\frac{d}{p}} and we set R⁡(x)=R0R(x)=R_{0}, or there exists 0<R⁡(x)≤R00<R(x)\leq R_{0} such that ‖∇u‖Lp​(Bd​(x,R⁡(x))∩Ω)=A​(R⁡(x))−3+α+dp\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B_{d}(x,R(x))\cap\Omega)}=A\,(R(x))^{-3+\alpha+\frac{d}{p}}.

The result then follows from Besicovitch covering Theorem by considering the balls Bd​(x,R​(x))B_{d}(x,R(x)) for each x∈Ωx\in\Omega. ∎

Proof of Proposition 9.

We consider (for p,q,αp,q,\alpha satisfying the conditions of the Proposition) functions u∈Wl​o​c1,p​(Ω)u\in\textnormal{W}^{1,p}_{loc}(\Omega), w∈𝒞α​(Ω¯)w\in\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{\Omega}). Here and in the rest of the proof, in the case when α=0\alpha=0, 𝒞α​(Ω¯)\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{\Omega}) is replaced by L∞​(Ω)\textnormal{L}^{\infty}(\Omega) (and the corresponding norm becomes the ∥∥∞\|\,\,\|_{\infty} norm).

Then we take A:=‖w‖𝒞α​(Ω¯)A:=\|w\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})} and use Lemma 23 in order to get a covering ℬ\mathcal{B} satisfying the conclusion of Lemma 23. By the covering, we find that

‖u‖Lq​(Ω)q≤∑B∈ℬ‖u‖Lq​(B∩Ω)q≤Cd,p,q,αq​∑B∈ℬ[R1−d⁡(1p−1q)​‖∇u‖Lp​(B∩Ω)+R−2+α+dq​‖w‖𝒞α​(B∩Ω¯)]q,\|u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(\Omega)}^{q}\leq\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}}\|u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(B\cap\Omega)}^{q}\leq C_{d,p,q,\alpha}^{q}\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}}\left[R^{1-d\left(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}\right)}\,\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B\cap\Omega)}+R^{-2+\alpha+\frac{d}{q}}\,\|w\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{B\cap\Omega})}\right]^{q},

where we applied in the last step (69) in Lemma 22 to each cut ball B∩ΩB\cap\Omega, with B∈ℬB\in\mathcal{B}.

For each ball B∈ℬB\in\mathcal{B}, the choice of RR implies in the case that R<R0R<R_{0} that

R1−d⁡(1p−1q)​‖∇u‖Lp​(B∩Ω)=R−2+α+dq​‖w‖𝒞α​(B∩Ω¯)=‖w‖𝒞α​(Ω¯)1−d⁡(1p−1q)3−α−d/p​‖∇u‖Lp​(B∩Ω)2−α−d/q3−α−d/p.R^{1-d\left(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}\right)}\,\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B\cap\Omega)}=R^{-2+\alpha+\frac{d}{q}}\,\|w\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{B\cap\Omega})}=\|w\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})}^{\frac{1-d\left(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}\right)}{3-\alpha-d/p}}\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B\cap\Omega)}^{\frac{2-\alpha-d/q}{3-\alpha-d/p}}.

The case R=R0R=R_{0} can only apply a fixed number of times as each such ball covers at least a fixed volume and by the covering the volume of all balls is bounded (as the domain is bounded). In this case

R1−d⁡(1p−1q)​‖∇u‖Lp​(B∩Ω)+R−2+α+dq​‖w‖𝒞α​(B∩Ω¯)≤‖w‖𝒞α​(Ω¯)1−d⁡(1p−1q)3−α−d/p​‖∇u‖Lp​(B∩Ω)2−α−d/q3−α−d/p+R0−2+α+dq​‖w‖𝒞α​(B∩Ω¯).R^{1-d\left(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}\right)}\,\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B\cap\Omega)}+R^{-2+\alpha+\frac{d}{q}}\,\|w\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{B\cap\Omega})}\leq\|w\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})}^{\frac{1-d\left(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}\right)}{3-\alpha-d/p}}\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B\cap\Omega)}^{\frac{2-\alpha-d/q}{3-\alpha-d/p}}+R_{0}^{-2+\alpha+\frac{d}{q}}\|w\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{B\cap\Omega})}.

Hence we find by the covering that (for a constant C>0C>0)

‖u‖Lq​(Ω)q≤C​‖w‖𝒞α​(Ω¯)q−d​q​(1p−1q)3−α−d/p​∑B∈ℬ‖∇u‖Lp​(B∩Ω)q⁡(2−α−d/q3−α−d/p)+C​‖w‖𝒞α​(Ω¯)q.\|u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{q}(\Omega)}^{q}\leq C\,\|w\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})}^{\frac{q-dq\left(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}\right)}{3-\alpha-d/p}}\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}}\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B\cap\Omega)}^{q\left(\frac{2-\alpha-d/q}{3-\alpha-d/p}\right)}+C\,\|w\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})}^{q}.

As the covering covers every point at most cdc_{d} times, and observing that (thanks to the assumption on p,q,αp,q,\alpha in the Proposition)

q⁡(2−α−dq3−α−dp)≥p,q\left(\frac{2-\alpha-\frac{d}{q}}{3-\alpha-\frac{d}{p}}\right)\geq p, (73)

we see that

∑B∈ℬ‖∇u‖Lp​(B∩Ω)q⁡(2−α−d/q3−α−d/p)≤∑B∈ℬ‖∇u‖Lp​(B∩Ω)p​‖∇u‖Lp​(Ω)q⁡(2−α−d/q3−α−d/p)−p≤cd​‖∇u‖Lp​(Ω)q⁡(2−α−d/q3−α−d/p),\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}}\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B\cap\Omega)}^{q\left(\frac{2-\alpha-d/q}{3-\alpha-d/p}\right)}\leq\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}}\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(B\cap\Omega)}^{p}\,\,\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(\Omega)}^{q\left(\frac{2-\alpha-d/q}{3-\alpha-d/p}\right)-p}\leq c_{d}\,\|\nabla u\|_{\textnormal{L}^{p}(\Omega)}^{q\left(\frac{2-\alpha-d/q}{3-\alpha-d/p}\right)},

which yields the sought interpolation. ∎
